title: Treatment and Outcomes of Sheltered Cats with Feline Panleukopenia using Canine Parvovirus Monoclonal Antibody (CPMA) [Abstract]
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
abstract: The researchers evaluated whether canine parvovirus monoclonal antibody (CPMA) could improve outcomes for shelter cats with feline panleukopenia. Among 55 diagnosed cats, 31 received standard care while 24 also received CPMA injections. Results showed median time to clinical resolution and treatment discontinuation was 3.5 days shorter for the CPMA-treated group. Overall survival reached 85.5%, with no statistically significant mortality difference between groups (CPMA: 20.8% vs. standard: 9.7%). The authors concluded that CPMA may be helpful for shelters seeking to reduce isolation treatment duration, noting no adverse effects were observed. (Conference proceedings abstract, JSMCAH Vol. 4 No. S1, published April 28, 2025.)
takeaways: Canine parvovirus monoclonal antibody (CPMA) shortened time to clinical resolution by ~3.5 days in shelter cats with feline panleukopenia and was well tolerated, which can reduce costly isolation length-of-stay and support capacity for care; however supportive care remains the mainstay and CPMA did not significantly change overall survival.

authors: Lenz OC, Powell L, Reinhard CL, Watson B
title: Short-term storage conditions do not affect canine fecal cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A concentrations
abstract: Fecal cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) are frequently used biomarkers in animal welfare, wildlife conservation, and other fields. However, these research settings often lack immediate access to a -80 degrees C freezer or other ultra-low temperature storage equipment. This study aims to determine whether canine fecal cortisol and sIgA concentrations remain stable over 24 h at either ambient temperature or on wet ice. Fecal samples were collected from 10 adult dogs housed in two Philadelphia area animal shelters in May and June of 2024. After aliquoting, baseline samples were frozen on dry ice within 15 minutes of defecation. Remaining aliquots were stored at ambient temperature (15-21 degrees C) or on wet ice (4 degrees C) for 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 hours before freezing on dry ice. Cortisol and sIgA concentrations were quantified using ELISAs and analyzed with a linear mixed effects model. No significant differences were found between time points or storage conditions. These data show that concentrations of fecal canine cortisol and sIgA remain stable if stored unfrozen for 24 hours. Immediate freezing at -80 degrees C does not appear to be necessary for accurate quantification of these analytes. This knowledge removes logistical and regulatory barriers to conducting quality noninvasive research in animal shelter, clinical, and field settings.
takeaways: Canine fecal cortisol and sIgA (noninvasive stress/immune welfare biomarkers) stay stable for 24 h at room temperature or on wet ice, so immediate -80 degrees C freezing is not required. This makes noninvasive welfare and stress research feasible in real-world shelter and field settings without specialized cold storage.

authors: Jafarian S, Powell L, Reinhard CL, Watson B
title: Shelter medicine rotations help students rethink care for underserved communities: a qualitative analysis of veterinary student reflective journals
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: The researchers examined how shelter medicine rotations influence veterinary student perspectives. They analyzed reflective journals from 53 students at the University of Pennsylvania's School of Veterinary Medicine between January 2015 and July 2019 using qualitative content analysis. Eight major themes emerged, including student perspectives of owners, pets, neighborhoods, community outreach, and self; the learning process; the role of pets as social catalysts; and trust. Students demonstrated meaningful shifts in how they viewed pet owners. The study found that community engagement, both in duration and variety, helped students develop critical interpersonal abilities including social competence, cultural humility, and contextualized decision-making. The authors conclude that structured, reflective community-based learning can enhance emotional intelligence and prepare students for serving diverse populations. They advocate for integrating sustained, diverse, and ethically grounded community engagement into veterinary curricula. (J Am Vet Med Assoc 2026; 264(4):476-484.)
takeaways: Shelter medicine / community-engagement rotations measurably shift veterinary students' attitudes toward pet owners in underserved communities, building cultural humility and contextualized decision-making. Supports the access-to-care and community-driven sheltering model as a core competency in veterinary education.

authors: Powell L, Graham K, Grant L, Lenz O, Reinhard CL, Yost H, Anderson E, Watson B
title: Insights into shelter dog outcomes using behavioral and biological stress markers
abstract: The research team investigated whether behavioral observations and stress biomarkers could help predict outcomes for shelter dogs. Over nine months, they studied 224 dogs from three Pennsylvania shelters, collecting fecal samples and recording behavioral videos at two timepoints (within 48 hours and 7-9 days after entry). Key findings indicated that at shelter entry, behavior patterns differed significantly by outcome. Dogs returned to owners demonstrated increased panting while those euthanized or transferred showed less time sitting than adopted dogs. After one week, human-directed behaviors became predictive; dogs that were adopted or transferred spent more time standing with their front paws on the cage and wagging tails compared to euthanized animals. Cortisol levels were higher in adopted versus transferred dogs at baseline but showed no significant difference by week one. Immunoglobulin A levels did not meaningfully correlate with outcomes. The authors concluded that in-kennel behavioral observations may provide the most useful information for shelters to assess stress, while biological markers warranted further investigation into how dogs adapt to shelter environments.
takeaways: In-kennel behavioral observation (e.g., human-directed behaviors at one week such as front paws on the cage and tail wagging) predicted shelter dog outcomes better than fecal cortisol or IgA, which correlated poorly. Practical, low-cost behavioral monitoring is more useful than biomarkers for assessing shelter dog stress and welfare.

authors: Garcia LC, Dietrich J, Watson B, Reinhard CL, Cole SD
title: Confirmation of Efficacy of Commonly Used Veterinary Surface Disinfectants Against Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales Isolated from Pets
journal: Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association
abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) are an emerging public health threat in both human and veterinary medicine. As antibiotic resistance grows, there is increased importance in preventing the spread and transmission of these organisms by using appropriate infection prevention and biosecurity measures. The goal of this study was to test the efficacy of commonly used disinfectants in the veterinary setting against CPE strains. A total of 10 bacterial strains (9 CPE and 1 control strain) and 5 disinfectants were evaluated. Effective disinfection (at least a 3-log kill) was found at the manufacturer's contact time for all strains when paired with all products except for one strain (47422-21) of Enterobacter hormaechei, which only had a 2-log for the accelerated hydrogen peroxide product and a 1-log reduction for the quaternary ammonium compound product. When used according to manufacturer recommendations, the five surface disinfectants tested were effective in vitro against the majority of CPE of animal origin that were evaluated. (J Am Anim Hosp Assoc 2025; 61(4):83-89; DOI 10.5326/JAAHA-MS-7440.)
takeaways: Five commonly used veterinary surface disinfectants achieved adequate (>=3-log) kill against most carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (an emerging multidrug-resistant, zoonotic biosecurity threat) when used at the manufacturer's labeled contact time. One Enterobacter hormaechei strain resisted accelerated hydrogen peroxide and quaternary ammonium, underscoring that correct contact time and product selection are critical for shelter/clinic biosecurity.

authors: Sensharma R, Reinhard CL, Powell L, Watson B
title: Public perceptions of free-roaming dogs and cats in India and the United States
journal: Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science
abstract: This cross-sectional investigation examined differences in how Indian and American communities perceive free-roaming canines and felines. Survey data from 498 respondents (210 Indian, 288 American) collected between August 2021 and February 2022 revealed that Indian participants largely viewed these animals as community members, with significantly greater support for allowing them to roam freely. Both groups expressed welfare concerns, though Americans were more likely to cite welfare, public health, and wildlife risks. American respondents favored adoption and euthanasia strategies, while Indian respondents preferred spay/neuter, vaccinate and release strategies for population management. The findings emphasize tailoring interventions to reflect local cultural values regarding free-roaming animal populations. (J Appl Anim Welf Sci 2025; 28(4):563-577; DOI 10.1080/10888705.2024.2374078.)
takeaways: Cultural context shapes free-roaming dog/cat management preferences: Indian respondents viewed them as community members and favored spay-neuter-vaccinate-release (TNVR-style), while US respondents favored adoption and euthanasia and cited public-health/wildlife risk. Effective community cat/dog and One Health population programs must be culturally tailored.

authors: Schumacher E, Berliner E, Hicks S, Aziz C, Wong Gordon E, Hedge Z, Hurley K, Reed J, Stuntebeck R
title: The Association of Shelter Veterinarians' Guidelines for Humane Rabbit Housing in Animal Shelters
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
abstract: The published article does not include a traditional structured abstract. Its stated purpose (from the Introduction) is: "The purpose of this document is to provide guidelines for the humane housing of rabbits in animal shelters, rescue groups, and foster homes, based on expert input and available scientific research." These first-of-their-kind Association of Shelter Veterinarians (ASV) consensus guidelines were developed by nearly two dozen rabbit-care, facility-design, and shelter-medicine experts over roughly three years and address enclosure design and size, cohousing/social housing, environmental enrichment, lighting, sanitation, and infectious disease management for sheltered rabbits. Listed keywords: rabbit welfare, animal shelter housing, environmental enrichment, species-specific care, capacity for care. (JSMCAH Vol. 4 No. S2, 2025; DOI 10.56771/jsmcah.v4.149.)
takeaways: First ASV consensus guidelines establishing species-specific humane housing standards for rabbits (the third most common shelter species), covering enclosure size, social cohousing, enrichment, lighting, sanitation, and infectious disease control. Extends the Capacity for Care framework beyond dogs/cats and is the go-to reference for shelter rabbit welfare standards.
